subject: Biology
title: Fight or Flight Response
description: A quick, practical guide to Fight or Flight Response.

hook.text: A rabbit spots a fox. In milliseconds, its heart rate spikes, muscles tense, and it bolts.

buildup.text: The fight-or-flight response floods the body with adrenaline, preparing for action.

discovery.text: Blood flow shifts to muscles. Digestion stops. Pupils dilate. Pain sensitivity drops.

twist.text: Some animals freeze instead—playing dead. Opossums go limp and even emit a corpse-like smell.

climax.text: This ancient response system exists in nearly all vertebrates, including humans.

punchline.text: Fight, flee, or freeze. Decide in a heartbeat.

quiz.question: What hormone drives the fight-or-flight response?

details.summary: The fight-or-flight response is an automatic physiological reaction to perceived threats. The sympathetic nervous system releases adrenaline, increasing heart rate, dilating pupils, and redirecting blood to muscles, preparing the animal for immediate action.
details.whyItMatters: This survival mechanism is shared across virtually all vertebrates and shapes behaviors from predator avoidance to territorial aggression. Understanding it connects neuroscience, physiology, and behavioral ecology.
takeaways: Adrenaline triggers rapid physiological changes for emergency action
The response diverts energy from digestion to muscles and alertness
Chronic activation of stress responses damages health in many species

faq.question: What triggers the fight-or-flight response?
faq.answer: The amygdala detects a threat and signals the hypothalamus, which activates the sympathetic nervous system. Adrenal glands release adrenaline and cortisol within seconds, preparing the body for explosive physical action.

faq.question: Do all animals have fight-or-flight responses?
faq.answer: Most vertebrates share this basic stress response. Many also exhibit a freeze response as a third option. Invertebrates have analogous systems using different chemistry but achieving similar rapid mobilization for survival threats.
